![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image} The First Law of Geography is that "everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things" Waldo Tobler. Quantitatively, this can be expressed as **spatial autocorrelation** -- the correlation of values in a variable by distance. Put in the context of Tobler's First Law of Geography, we might expect that values associated with spatial objects that are close to one another are more similar than those that are further apart. Of course, the distance in which values are correlated will depend on the variable you are studying. In this video lesson (runtime: 49:28) we will explore the all-important concept of spatial autocorrelation (see the classic paper "[Spatial Autocorrelation: Trouble or New Paradigm?](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/1939924){target="blank"}"; Legendre 1993) and how to address it in your data. Specifically, we will cover: * What spatial autocorrelation is * How to detect spatial autocorrelation in a sample * How to *avoid* spatial autocorrelation in you study design * How to test for spatial autocorrelation in your model results * How to *use* spatial autocorrelation! *Note: Much of this video lesson is quite complex and you will not be evaluated on most of the material herein. Material that you will be evaluated on includes purrr's `keep()` function, `terra::ext()`, and `terra::aggregate()`.*
Please click on the buttons below to explore the metadata for this lesson! ::: panel **[birds_cicadas_lc.rds]{.mono}**: This is the list of files that we used in the categorize video. For this module, we will only use: - [nlcd_key]{.mono}: A key to the National Land Cover Database classified raster that includes the land cover class (id), the class name, color value intended to be used for a class, and the class description. If you work with spatial data, this might be really handy to have! **[dc_census.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a polygon shapefile (EPSG 32618; UTM Zone 18N) from the US Census Bureau that provides tract-level census data for the District of Columbia. The data were downloaded using the tigris and tidycensus packages in R. **[dc_crimes.csv]{.mono}**: This is a tabular that provides the location and types of crimes in the District of Columbia from 2019-2021. The data were collected with the CRS EPSG 4326 and downloaded from Open Data DC. **[dc_forests.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a polygon shapefile of forested land in Washington DC. Each polygon represents an individual forest and represent a subset of the original file (to polygon areas greater than 9 hectares). The data were obtained from Open Data DC and the CRS is EPSG 4326. See the original metadata at this link. **[dc_land.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a multipolygon shapefile of land (as opposed to water) in Washington DC. We made this (or something very similar) in one of the earlier video lessons. The CRS is projected (NAD83/Conus Albers; EPSG 5070). **[dc_rivers.geojson]{.mono}**:This is a polygon shapefile of water bodies that are classified as "River" in Washington DC. The data were derived from the Water Bodies shapefile obtained from Open Data DC and the CRS is EPSG 4326. See the original metadata at this link. **[dc_stack.tif]{.mono}**: This is geotiff a raster stack of land cover files from Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC). The resolution of the stack is 30 by 30 meters and the CRS of the object is EPSG 5070. Layers include canopy (propoertion of canopy cover), imp (proportion of impervious surface), nlcd (classified land cover of each cell), and land (binary raster representing cells over land (as opposed to water). **[dc_street_trees.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a point shapefile of georeferenced street trees in Washington DC. Each point represents a single tree. Because the file is rather large, I subset the data to only trees where the crown area was greater than the median crown area across trees (n = 174,305 trees). The data were obtained from Open Data DC and are in an unprojected coordinate system (datum = WGS84). See the original metadata at this link. **[dc_tmax.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster of maximum July temperatures in the greater Washington DC region, averaged over a 30-year period. These data were modeled by, and obtained from, the Prism Climate Group at Oregon State University (link). The resolution of these data are roughly 800 x 800 m and the CRS is unprojected (EPSG 4269). **[dem_dc_10m.tif]{.mono}**: This is geotiff raster of elevation in Washington DC. Elevation values are provided in meters above sea level. The data were obtained from the National Map. The resolution of the raster is approximately 9 x 9 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (NAD83/Conus Albers). **[inat_scbi.geojson]{.mono}**: iNaturalist point shapefile observations from the campus of the Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation in 2024. The data were downloaded using the R package *rinat* and are in the unprojected coordinate reference system EPSG 4326. **[roads_scbi.geojson]{.mono}**: Linestring shapefile of roads within the spatial extent of the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute. The data were obtained using the [National Map download tool](https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/){target="_blank"} and are in an unprojected CRS (EPSG 4326). **[scbi_canopy_cover.tif]{.mono}**: Proportion of canopy cover within a 30m resolution map pixel, subset to the spatial extent of the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute. The data were obtained using the [MRLC viewer tool](https://www.mrlc.gov/viewer/){target="_blank} and are in an unprojected CRS (EPSG 4269). **[scbi_dem.tif]{.mono}**: Digital elevation model (raster; 10m resolution), subset to the spatial extent of the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute. The data were obtained using the [National Map download tool](https://apps.nationalmap.gov/downloader/){target="_blank"} and are in an unprojected CRS (EPSG 4269). **[scbi_lc.tif]{.mono}**: Classified land cover (raster; 1m resolution), subset to the spatial extent of the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute. The data were obtained using the [Chesapeake Conservancy tool](https://cicgis.org/portal/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=bdf7ca3e249a40fd9a9d83d6e16100ea&extent=-88.252,35.0981,-62.3462,45.7489){target="_blank"} and are in an unprojected CRS (EPSG 4269) **[smsc_campus_scbi.geojson]{.mono}**: Shapefile that describes the boundaries of the Smithsonian-Mason-School of Conservation campus. Brian digitized this file by hand (poorly) and the data are in an unprojected CRS (EPSG 4326). **[birds_cicadas_lc.rds]{.mono}**: The data are formatted as a list of tibble data frames. The only one we will use for this lesson is [nlcd_key]{.mono}, which is a key to the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) Consortium](https://www.mrlc.gov/){target="_blank"} land cover classes. Fields in this list item include: * [id]{.mono}, numeric: The value assigned to each land cover class. * [name]{.mono}, character: A name assigned to each land cover class. * [color_value]{.mono}, character: The recommended color to use for each land cover class. * [description]{.mono}, character: A description of the type of land cover that each land cover class represents. **[canopy_cover.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the canopy cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by tree canopy. The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[dc_census.geojson]{.mono}**: A polygon shapefile of census tracts in the District of Columbia. The data are in a projected coordinate system (datum = WGS84, projection is UTM, Zone 18N) with the EPSG code 32618. The data include the following fields: * [GEOID]{.mono}, character: The **primary key** key for each census tract. * [STATEFP]{.mono}, character: A **foreign key** to the US state in the [states]{.mono} data. * [ALAND]{.mono}, numeric: The area covered by land in each census tract, in square meters. * [AWATER]{.mono}, numeric: The area covered by water in each census tract, in square meters. * [INCOME]{.mono}, numeric: The median income of each census tract. * [POPULATION]{.mono}, numeric: The total population of each census tract. **[dc_crimes.csv]{.mono}**: Crime data were obtained from Open Data DC. This is a tabular dataset and each row represents the record for an individual crime committed. Relevant fields (columns) include: * [id]{.mono}, character: The primary key for each observation; * [offense]{.mono}, character: The type of crime committed; **[impervious_surface.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the impervious surface cover cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by man-made materials (pavement, sidewalks, rooftops). The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[nlcd.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the land cover in the greater Washington DC region. Values are categorical and each value represents the dominant land cover class (link) of each cell. The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[sick_birds.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a point shapefile that represents sick birds that were brought to City Wildlife, a wildlife rehabilitation center in the District of Columbia, in the spring of 2021. These data were obtained directly from City Wildlife staff. Location information for birds brought into the center were obtained by Brian through geocoding addresses via the Google Maps API with the R package *ggmap*. The CRS for these data is EPSG 4326. * [patient_id]{.mono}, character: The **primary key** for each patient, assigned to bird upon intake. * [admission_date]{.mono}, date: The date that a bird was brought to City Wildlife. * [common_name]{.mono}, character: The common name for the species of bird. * [age]{.mono}, character: The age of a given bird. * [attitude]{.mono}, character: Behavioral observations of a given bird upon intake ::: ## Video lesson Notes: * You will see me complain about my usage of hanging parentheses ... but that is now (usually) my preference! * Your script will not exactly match my video script. Wherever possible, I have modified the script to adhere to the course style guide (e.g., indentation) and replaced single quotes with double quotes. * In the video I call the script `advanced_rasters_2.R`. This was not appropriately named because many of the analyses in this script have little to do with rasters (directly at least). As such, the script file you will use for this lesson is `spatial_autocorrelation.r`. {{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/PCPTI0Pw76w >}} ## Addendum: A closer look at raster aggregation We used `terra::aggregate()` in the video above to change a raster to a coarser resolution. Unfortunately, I did a very bad job of explaining how to do so. As such, I decided to provide a bit more explanation. Let's set up a new session for a quick exploration of `terra::aggregate()`: ```{r, warning = FALSE,message = FALSE} library(sf) library(tmap) library(tidyverse) # Set tmap to "view" for the entire session: tmap_mode("view") # Read in the digital elevation model raster data: dem <- terra::rast("data/raw/rasters/dem_dc_10m.tif") # Read in dc_land: dc_land <- st_read( "data/raw/shapefiles/dc_land.geojson", quiet = TRUE ) ``` For our example, I will use `terra::spatSample()` to generate 5,000 random point samples within the spatial extent of `dem` and convert the points to *sf* files: ```{r} rando_points <- dem %>% terra::spatSample( size = 5000, method = "random", as.points = TRUE, values = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE ) %>% st_as_sf() ``` Let's have a look at our point and raster data on a map: ```{r} # Add the elevation model: dem %>% tm_shape(name = "Elevation") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Elevation") ) + # Add random points: rando_points %>% tm_shape(name = "Rando points") + tm_dots() ``` You will notice that the we received the warning message "stars object downsampled to ...". We have seen that warning message a lot. It means that the raster has been modified to a courser resolution. Rather than letting *tmap* modify our resolution for us, we can do so directly with `terra::aggregate()`. We supply (at a minimum): * `x = ...`: The target raster; * `fact = ...`: An integer value specifying the number of cells in each direction to aggregate (*Note: There are other options, but I rarely use them*); * `fun = ...`: The function used to aggregate the values (i.e., since the cells have different values, we need to know how to combine those values for the new raster cells). In the code below, I aggregate `dem` by a factor of 4 and use the function `mean` to combine the values: ```{r} dem_agg <- dem %>% terra::aggregate( fact = 4, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE ) ``` Let's look at the metadata of the two rasters to compare the original and aggregated cell sizes: ```{r} dem dem_agg ``` We can see that the resolution of the original raster was about 9.2 meters whereas the resolution of the aggregated raster is almost 37 meters! Moreover, our new raster has considerably fewer cells, so we can now plot data without a warning message: ```{r} # Add the elevation model: dem_agg %>% tm_shape(name = "Elevation") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Elevation") ) + # Add random points: rando_points %>% tm_shape(name = "Rando points") + tm_dots() ``` This operation can also be analytically useful. For example, perhaps we might want to count the number of observations per raster cell -- in doing so, the resolution of cells can really make a difference. We can use `terra::rasterize()` to do so. Below, let's count the number of sampling points per raster cell (`fun = "length"`) using the original ~10m resolution digital elevation model: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell") ) ``` We can see from the legend that there are some values that are not zero, but you really have to zoom in to see those locations. Additionally, the maximum value is "1" suggesting that there is no more than one point per cell. We can improve this a little bit by using an aggregated raster: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the aggregated dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem_agg, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell") ) ``` But the level of improvement is minimal -- there are now more points per raster cell, however points are still rather difficult to observe. We can improve this by aggregating the data even further. I like to aim towards a target resolution that might make sense. For example, perhaps my goal is to determine the number of samples per square kilometer (1 km^2^ is 1000 x 1000m). I can use the resolution of the current raster cells to determine how many cells I need to aggregate. We can use `terra::res()` to return a vector with the x and y resolution of a raster: ```{r} terra::res(dem) ``` We can then (roughly) determine the number of cells that need to be aggregated to achieve that resolution: ```{r} 1000 / terra::res(dem)[[1]] ``` *Note: Because the x and y values of the resolution are equivalent, I use `[[...]]` to extract just one of the values.* Rounding this, we can see that we need to aggregate the data by a factor of `109` to generate raster cells of roughly 1 km^2^. Below, I rasterize based on the original raster with `fun = "length"` and then aggregate the resultant data with `fact = 109` (109 cells in the horizontal and vertical dimensions) and `fun = "sum"`: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell # (at a course resolution): terra::aggregate( fact = 109, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per square kilometer") ) ``` Be sure to use the metadata to check the new resolution of the aggregated raster: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell # (at a course resolution): terra::aggregate( fact = 109, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE ) ``` ## Reference ::: panel - **Distance matrix**: For shapefiles, this represents the pairwise distances between each feature, and often the pairwise distances between values of each feature. - **Endogenous autocorrelation**: Autocorrelation generated within a variable itself. - **Exogenous autocorrelation**: Autocorrelation generated by an outside variable; typically caused by something in the environment which is itself autocorrelated. - **Global Moran's I**: Spatial autocorrelation across all values in a data set. - **Inverse distance matrix**: The degree of similarity between points; Weigh points based on how close they are, with closer points receiving a higher weight (This is similar to an inverse distance matrix). - **Inverse-distance-weighting (IDW) model**: An interpolation method that calculates a weighted average where locations that are closer to a target cell have a larger impact on the assigned value of that cell. - **Kriging model**: An interpolation method that uses a semivariogram to weigh the predicted values based on the scale of spatial autocorrelation in the data. - **Lag distance**: The pairwise distances between each point in the system. - **Moran's correlogram**: A method used to calculate the degree of spatial autocorrelation at given pairwise distance classes. - **Moran's I statistic**: Represents the degree of similarity in space (how spatially dependent the data are). - **Negative spatial autocorrelation**: Near values are less similar than would be expected by random chance. - **Neighbors weights object**: The degree of similarity between polygons; Weigh polygons based on how close they are, with closer polygons receiving a higher weight (This is similar to an inverse distance matrix). - **Nugget**: The expected difference in semivariance between infinitesimally close distances. If spatial processes are the only determinant of variance in the data, then we would expect the nugget to be zero. - **Positive spatial autocorrelation**: Near values are more similar than far values. - **Range**: The distance between points at which we consider samples to be spatially independent. - **Semivariance**: The proportion of total variance explained at a given distance between sample locations. In other words, this represents the degree of dissimilarity in the measured variable between points. - **Semivariogram**: A type of plot used to assess the scale at which a variable is spatially independent. - **Sill**: The value of semivariance when samples are spatially independent. - **Spatial autocorrelation**: Systematic spatial variation in a variable. ::: ::: panel ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [**Important!**]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} * Primitive functions, as well as functions in the *base*, *stats*, and *utils* packages, are loaded by default when you start an R session. Functions in *dplyr*, *ggplot2*, *lubridate*, *purrr*, *readr*, *stringr*, *tibble*, *tidyr*, and *tidyverse* are loaded with `library(tidyverse)`. * I do not include functions that I recommend avoiding. * Regular expressions metacharacters are not functions! ::: ::: function_table ```{r, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE} render_function_table("functions_7.2_spatial_autocorrelation.csv") ``` ::: ::: ::: panel ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Metacharacters are not R functions!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} When you are given a list of functions that you may use in a given problem set, recall that regex metacharacters are not functions. As such, they will not be included in your function list. You may use *any* metacharacter to address a given problem! ::: * **Alternation constraint**, `(...)`: Constrains the use of a metacharacter to just the symbols inside of parentheses * **Anchor**, `^...`: Specify the start of a string * **Anchor**, `...$`: Specify the end of a string * **Character class**, `[...]`: Define a *set* of symbols that you would like to match * **Metacharacter escape**, `\\`: Treat a metacharacter as a literal character * **Optional match**, `?`: Specify that the preceding symbol is optional * **Range** (in a character class), `[...-...]`: Define a *range* of symbols that you would like to match in a given position * **Or**, `...|...`: Specify a match of one string "or" another string * **Repetition**, `...*`: Specify that a symbol can appear no times or an unlimited number of times * **Repetition**, `...+`: Specify that a symbol appears at least once or an unlimited number of times * **Repetition**, `{...}`: Specify the number of times a symbol should appear * **Repetition**, `{...,...}`: Specify that a symbol may appear within a range of repetitions * **Wild card**, `.`: Specify that a character value at a given location can be any symbol ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/keyboard_shortcuts.qmd >}} ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/rstudio_panes.qmd >}} :::

The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[dc_census.geojson]{.mono}**: A polygon shapefile of census tracts in the District of Columbia. The data are in a projected coordinate system (datum = WGS84, projection is UTM, Zone 18N) with the EPSG code 32618. The data include the following fields: * [GEOID]{.mono}, character: The **primary key** key for each census tract. * [STATEFP]{.mono}, character: A **foreign key** to the US state in the [states]{.mono} data. * [ALAND]{.mono}, numeric: The area covered by land in each census tract, in square meters. * [AWATER]{.mono}, numeric: The area covered by water in each census tract, in square meters. * [INCOME]{.mono}, numeric: The median income of each census tract. * [POPULATION]{.mono}, numeric: The total population of each census tract. **[dc_crimes.csv]{.mono}**: Crime data were obtained from Open Data DC. This is a tabular dataset and each row represents the record for an individual crime committed. Relevant fields (columns) include: * [id]{.mono}, character: The primary key for each observation; * [offense]{.mono}, character: The type of crime committed; **[impervious_surface.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the impervious surface cover cover in the greater Washington DC region. Cell values are continuous and represent the percentage of each cell that is covered by man-made materials (pavement, sidewalks, rooftops). The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[nlcd.tif]{.mono}**: This is a geotiff raster obtained from the [Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics Consortium (MRLC)](https://www.mrlc.gov/data){target="_blank"} that describes the land cover in the greater Washington DC region. Values are categorical and each value represents the dominant land cover class (link) of each cell. The resolution of the raster is approximately 30 x 30 m and the CRS is EPSG 5070 (datum = NAD83; projection = Albers Equal Area). **[sick_birds.geojson]{.mono}**: This is a point shapefile that represents sick birds that were brought to City Wildlife, a wildlife rehabilitation center in the District of Columbia, in the spring of 2021. These data were obtained directly from City Wildlife staff. Location information for birds brought into the center were obtained by Brian through geocoding addresses via the Google Maps API with the R package *ggmap*. The CRS for these data is EPSG 4326. * [patient_id]{.mono}, character: The **primary key** for each patient, assigned to bird upon intake. * [admission_date]{.mono}, date: The date that a bird was brought to City Wildlife. * [common_name]{.mono}, character: The common name for the species of bird. * [age]{.mono}, character: The age of a given bird. * [attitude]{.mono}, character: Behavioral observations of a given bird upon intake ::: ## Video lesson Notes: * You will see me complain about my usage of hanging parentheses ... but that is now (usually) my preference! * Your script will not exactly match my video script. Wherever possible, I have modified the script to adhere to the course style guide (e.g., indentation) and replaced single quotes with double quotes. * In the video I call the script `advanced_rasters_2.R`. This was not appropriately named because many of the analyses in this script have little to do with rasters (directly at least). As such, the script file you will use for this lesson is `spatial_autocorrelation.r`. {{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/PCPTI0Pw76w >}} ## Addendum: A closer look at raster aggregation We used `terra::aggregate()` in the video above to change a raster to a coarser resolution. Unfortunately, I did a very bad job of explaining how to do so. As such, I decided to provide a bit more explanation. Let's set up a new session for a quick exploration of `terra::aggregate()`: ```{r, warning = FALSE,message = FALSE} library(sf) library(tmap) library(tidyverse) # Set tmap to "view" for the entire session: tmap_mode("view") # Read in the digital elevation model raster data: dem <- terra::rast("data/raw/rasters/dem_dc_10m.tif") # Read in dc_land: dc_land <- st_read( "data/raw/shapefiles/dc_land.geojson", quiet = TRUE ) ``` For our example, I will use `terra::spatSample()` to generate 5,000 random point samples within the spatial extent of `dem` and convert the points to *sf* files: ```{r} rando_points <- dem %>% terra::spatSample( size = 5000, method = "random", as.points = TRUE, values = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE ) %>% st_as_sf() ``` Let's have a look at our point and raster data on a map: ```{r} # Add the elevation model: dem %>% tm_shape(name = "Elevation") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Elevation") ) + # Add random points: rando_points %>% tm_shape(name = "Rando points") + tm_dots() ``` You will notice that the we received the warning message "stars object downsampled to ...". We have seen that warning message a lot. It means that the raster has been modified to a courser resolution. Rather than letting *tmap* modify our resolution for us, we can do so directly with `terra::aggregate()`. We supply (at a minimum): * `x = ...`: The target raster; * `fact = ...`: An integer value specifying the number of cells in each direction to aggregate (*Note: There are other options, but I rarely use them*); * `fun = ...`: The function used to aggregate the values (i.e., since the cells have different values, we need to know how to combine those values for the new raster cells). In the code below, I aggregate `dem` by a factor of 4 and use the function `mean` to combine the values: ```{r} dem_agg <- dem %>% terra::aggregate( fact = 4, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE ) ``` Let's look at the metadata of the two rasters to compare the original and aggregated cell sizes: ```{r} dem dem_agg ``` We can see that the resolution of the original raster was about 9.2 meters whereas the resolution of the aggregated raster is almost 37 meters! Moreover, our new raster has considerably fewer cells, so we can now plot data without a warning message: ```{r} # Add the elevation model: dem_agg %>% tm_shape(name = "Elevation") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = terrain.colors(20)), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Elevation") ) + # Add random points: rando_points %>% tm_shape(name = "Rando points") + tm_dots() ``` This operation can also be analytically useful. For example, perhaps we might want to count the number of observations per raster cell -- in doing so, the resolution of cells can really make a difference. We can use `terra::rasterize()` to do so. Below, let's count the number of sampling points per raster cell (`fun = "length"`) using the original ~10m resolution digital elevation model: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell") ) ``` We can see from the legend that there are some values that are not zero, but you really have to zoom in to see those locations. Additionally, the maximum value is "1" suggesting that there is no more than one point per cell. We can improve this a little bit by using an aggregated raster: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the aggregated dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem_agg, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per raster cell") ) ``` But the level of improvement is minimal -- there are now more points per raster cell, however points are still rather difficult to observe. We can improve this by aggregating the data even further. I like to aim towards a target resolution that might make sense. For example, perhaps my goal is to determine the number of samples per square kilometer (1 km^2^ is 1000 x 1000m). I can use the resolution of the current raster cells to determine how many cells I need to aggregate. We can use `terra::res()` to return a vector with the x and y resolution of a raster: ```{r} terra::res(dem) ``` We can then (roughly) determine the number of cells that need to be aggregated to achieve that resolution: ```{r} 1000 / terra::res(dem)[[1]] ``` *Note: Because the x and y values of the resolution are equivalent, I use `[[...]]` to extract just one of the values.* Rounding this, we can see that we need to aggregate the data by a factor of `109` to generate raster cells of roughly 1 km^2^. Below, I rasterize based on the original raster with `fun = "length"` and then aggregate the resultant data with `fact = 109` (109 cells in the horizontal and vertical dimensions) and `fun = "sum"`: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell # (at a course resolution): terra::aggregate( fact = 109, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE ) %>% # Mask the resultant raster: terra::mask(dc_land) %>% # Plot the data: tm_shape(name = "Rasterized points") + tm_raster( col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(), col.legend = tm_legend(title = "Points per square kilometer") ) ``` Be sure to use the metadata to check the new resolution of the aggregated raster: ```{r} # Rasterize the points to the original dem raster: rando_points %>% terra::rasterize( y = dem, fun = "length", background = 0 ) %>% # Aggregate the resultant raster by counting the number of samples per cell # (at a course resolution): terra::aggregate( fact = 109, fun = "sum", na.rm = TRUE ) ``` ## Reference ::: panel - **Distance matrix**: For shapefiles, this represents the pairwise distances between each feature, and often the pairwise distances between values of each feature. - **Endogenous autocorrelation**: Autocorrelation generated within a variable itself. - **Exogenous autocorrelation**: Autocorrelation generated by an outside variable; typically caused by something in the environment which is itself autocorrelated. - **Global Moran's I**: Spatial autocorrelation across all values in a data set. - **Inverse distance matrix**: The degree of similarity between points; Weigh points based on how close they are, with closer points receiving a higher weight (This is similar to an inverse distance matrix). - **Inverse-distance-weighting (IDW) model**: An interpolation method that calculates a weighted average where locations that are closer to a target cell have a larger impact on the assigned value of that cell. - **Kriging model**: An interpolation method that uses a semivariogram to weigh the predicted values based on the scale of spatial autocorrelation in the data. - **Lag distance**: The pairwise distances between each point in the system. - **Moran's correlogram**: A method used to calculate the degree of spatial autocorrelation at given pairwise distance classes. - **Moran's I statistic**: Represents the degree of similarity in space (how spatially dependent the data are). - **Negative spatial autocorrelation**: Near values are less similar than would be expected by random chance. - **Neighbors weights object**: The degree of similarity between polygons; Weigh polygons based on how close they are, with closer polygons receiving a higher weight (This is similar to an inverse distance matrix). - **Nugget**: The expected difference in semivariance between infinitesimally close distances. If spatial processes are the only determinant of variance in the data, then we would expect the nugget to be zero. - **Positive spatial autocorrelation**: Near values are more similar than far values. - **Range**: The distance between points at which we consider samples to be spatially independent. - **Semivariance**: The proportion of total variance explained at a given distance between sample locations. In other words, this represents the degree of dissimilarity in the measured variable between points. - **Semivariogram**: A type of plot used to assess the scale at which a variable is spatially independent. - **Sill**: The value of semivariance when samples are spatially independent. - **Spatial autocorrelation**: Systematic spatial variation in a variable. ::: ::: panel ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [**Important!**]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} * Primitive functions, as well as functions in the *base*, *stats*, and *utils* packages, are loaded by default when you start an R session. Functions in *dplyr*, *ggplot2*, *lubridate*, *purrr*, *readr*, *stringr*, *tibble*, *tidyr*, and *tidyverse* are loaded with `library(tidyverse)`. * I do not include functions that I recommend avoiding. * Regular expressions metacharacters are not functions! ::: ::: function_table ```{r, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE} render_function_table("functions_7.2_spatial_autocorrelation.csv") ``` ::: ::: ::: panel ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}} [Metacharacters are not R functions!]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} When you are given a list of functions that you may use in a given problem set, recall that regex metacharacters are not functions. As such, they will not be included in your function list. You may use *any* metacharacter to address a given problem! ::: * **Alternation constraint**, `(...)`: Constrains the use of a metacharacter to just the symbols inside of parentheses * **Anchor**, `^...`: Specify the start of a string * **Anchor**, `...$`: Specify the end of a string * **Character class**, `[...]`: Define a *set* of symbols that you would like to match * **Metacharacter escape**, `\\`: Treat a metacharacter as a literal character * **Optional match**, `?`: Specify that the preceding symbol is optional * **Range** (in a character class), `[...-...]`: Define a *range* of symbols that you would like to match in a given position * **Or**, `...|...`: Specify a match of one string "or" another string * **Repetition**, `...*`: Specify that a symbol can appear no times or an unlimited number of times * **Repetition**, `...+`: Specify that a symbol appears at least once or an unlimited number of times * **Repetition**, `{...}`: Specify the number of times a symbol should appear * **Repetition**, `{...,...}`: Specify that a symbol may appear within a range of repetitions * **Wild card**, `.`: Specify that a character value at a given location can be any symbol ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/keyboard_shortcuts.qmd >}} ::: ::: panel {{< include ../../src/includes/rstudio_panes.qmd >}} :::
